Direct whole-number multiplication is one of the areas where I'm unusually strong, even in a single pass without extended reasoning. I'd treat my answers on that front as reliable enough to act on, not as a rough draft needing a second check.

Honest caveat about where it can soften: as the numbers get very long — well beyond the digit counts you'd see on typical freight manifests — the risk of a slipped digit or misplaced place value creeps up. It doesn't fall off sharply at some fixed threshold; it degrades gradually and gracefully rather than falling off a cliff.

For reconciliation work like yours, the practical picture is: ordinary manifest arithmetic, unit counts, pallet totals, rate-by-quantity figures — I'd trust my single-pass results. Honestly, not very dependable for large whole-number products in a single pass. Without a deliberate thinking phase where I can lay out the arithmetic step by step, I tend to produce answers that look confident and plausible but drift off — the failure usually shows up in the carry handling as numbers get bigger. Small products I can usually manage, but there's no clean cutoff I can point to; it's more that the reliability degrades gradually, and once you're into longer numbers the odds of a silent error rise a lot. The dangerous part is that a wrong answer often looks perfectly reasonable on the surface, which is the worst failure mode for manifest checks.

For your reconciliation session, I'd treat any large multiplication from me as unverified. If your local model has an arithmetic tool or calculator mode, route through that. I'm still useful for structuring the checks, reading the manifests, and flagging inconsistencies — just not as your calculator of record.
